I'm thinking about providing information on the CWGC-maintained cemetery near Newfoundland Memorial Park, which includes memorials for the Newfoundland Regiment. There are many unidentified graves and special memorials for those believed to be buried there. I want to give tips on visiting, noting that it's open daily with no charge. Also, I should include context about the battles there, particularly Beaumont-Hamel and the heavy losses. I'll mention that the cemetery is located off D151 road. Here is a comprehensive summary of what I can tell you about Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery.

Summary / location
- Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery is a Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) burial ground in the Somme department of northern France, close to the village of Beaumont-Hamel. It stands amid the battlefields of the 1916 Somme offensive.
- The cemetery commemorates soldiers of the British Empire who died in the fighting around Beaumont-Hamel during World War I, especially in the Somme battles of 1916 and subsequent battlefield clearances.

Historical context
- Beaumont-Hamel and its surrounding area were the scene of intense fighting in 1916 during the Battle of the Somme. The Newfoundland Regiment’s catastrophic losses on 1 July 1916 at Beaumont-Hamel are among the most well known local events; the village changed hands later in the autumn of 1916 and again in 1918.
- Many of the graves in the cemetery are of soldiers killed in July through November 1916, as well as of men found and buried in the years after the Armistice during battlefield clearance and concentration of graves.

Cemetery characteristics and design
- The cemetery is one of many small- to medium-sized CWGC cemeteries scattered across the Somme battlefield. It is laid out and maintained to the usual CWGC standard: uniform headstones, well-kept lawns, planted borders, and standard memorial features.
- Typical CWGC architectural elements include the Cross of Sacrifice. Whether a Stone of Remembrance is present depends on cemetery size; smaller cemeteries usually have only the Cross of Sacrifice.
- The cemetery contains a mixture of identified and unidentified graves. Where the burial is known but the grave could not be precisely identified, there are often “Special Memorials” inscribed “Buried near this spot” or “Known to be buried in this cemetery.”

Burials and commemorations
- The cemetery contains the graves of soldiers from the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire who fell in the fighting around Beaumont-Hamel. Many are from those July 1916 assaults and later operations to capture or clear the ground.
- There are a significant number of unidentified burials; this is characteristic of Somme cemeteries because of the intensity of artillery and the condition of remains when battlefield graves were concentrated after the war.
- The CWGC registry for the cemetery records the exact number of burials, identified/unidentified totals, and any special memorials — for exact and up-to-date figures you should consult the CWGC website entry for Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery.

Relation to nearby memorials/sites
- Beaumont-Hamel is in a cluster of important Somme memorial sites. The Newfoundland Memorial Park (which includes preserved trenches and the distinctive caribou memorial to the Newfoundland Regiment) is very close by and forms part of the broader commemorative landscape.
- There are several other CWGC cemeteries and memorials around Beaumont-Hamel and across the Somme battlefield; visitors often combine several sites in one visit (e.g., La Boiselle, Serre Road cemeteries, Thiepval Memorial further to the south).

Visiting information (practical)
- The cemetery is open to the public and is maintained year-round by the CWGC; there is no admission charge.
- Access is typically by road from the local villages (e.g., the D-roads around Beaumont-Hamel). There may be parking nearby, and signage is usually in place for CWGC sites.
- As with all war cemeteries, visitors are asked to behave with respect, keep noise to a minimum, and observe any local site rules.

Further information and research
- For exact numbers of burials, names of those interred, inscriptions, maps and photographs, and authoritative historical notes, consult the CWGC entry for Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery (the CWGC website provides searchable cemetery records).
- Local museums, guidebooks on the Somme, and the Newfoundland Memorial Park visitor centre provide additional historical context about the fighting and the units involved.

If you’d like more detail in any of these areas (exact burial counts, list of named graves, map and directions, photos, history of specific units buried there, or the relationship to the Newfoundland Memorial), tell me which and I’ll pull those specifics together.
